name: Fatima Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on a crew building a new line out to a solar farm on the flats past Saltmarsh, so it's new poles, new cross-arms and a lot of wind. I'm a first-year apprentice, so I do the ground work: framing the cross-arms on the ground before they go up, running the pulling rope, keeping the site tidy, checking the drawings. I start at seven and I'm usually the one who's read the job pack the night before, because I make my phone's AI assistant quiz me on it over dinner. I love building something new that will carry clean power for forty years. What wears me out is that my hands are slower than my brain, and at fifty-eight my hands aren't getting faster.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to the trade so late?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a cleaning business for eleven years, eight staff at the peak, and it went under in 2022 when we lost the two big office contracts. I'm still paying off the business loan, which is why there's never more than a couple of weeks of money in the account. My daughter Amira was studying electrical engineering and kept talking about the grid and all the new lines it needs, and I thought, well, why not me. My husband Joel thought I'd gone mad; now he brags about me at the school where he's caretaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because there were some really useful bits, and we let the companies oversell it. At work I'd probably admit I still use it every day for studying, and the lads would tease me. Online I'd post that the real story was always the grid, not the chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes, and that's fine. I'd still be paying off the loan and still learning, and the grid still needs building out to all these solar farms. Honestly, I'd miss the hype a little, it made things exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my apprenticeship and keep using the AI to study for my exams, because it's already helping. I'd keep chipping away at the loan; there's eighteen months left on it. Maybe I'd look into the drone pilot course the company offers, because drone inspection is useful whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like a film that didn't have an ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you study with AI every day. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week it was sag calculations, how much a line droops between poles in summer heat. I took a photo of the page in the manual, asked it to explain it three different ways, then made it set me five practice questions. Then I checked my answers with Mick, our foreman, because I'm not trusting it with a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Eighteen months on the loan. What happens when it's paid off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally have some breathing room, maybe three hundred a month. Part of it goes into savings, part into my pension, because I've got almost nothing in there from the business years. And one weekend away with Joel, somewhere with no wind.

S0.say: It's a shame the companies oversold AI, because some parts were really useful. She would admit to using it daily for study and say online that the real story was always the grid.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for her: she is still paying off a business loan and still learning. She would miss the excitement of the hype a little.
S0.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship and keeps studying with AI. Pays down the eighteen months left on her business loan and looks into the company's drone pilot course.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, like a film without an ending.
S0.quote: Honestly, I'd miss the hype a little, it made things exciting.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is genuinely curious about technology and already uses AI daily as a study partner. Her thin savings come from paying off a failed business, not from careless spending. She checks AI answers with her foreman, showing a sensible line between curiosity and safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need rules and the unions at the table, so the gains get shared and it's not just the shareholders. At work I'd tell people to learn the tools now, because the ones who do will be fine. Online I'd probably write a long post that nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it could be good for me. My hands are slow, but my brain's fine and I'm comfortable with the tech, so if the job shifts toward running drones and reading sensor data, I'm in a better spot than some of the old hands. The building work will still need people for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the drone pilot course in the first month and ask to be on the inspection trials. I'd join the union's technology working group if they have one, or ask them to start one. I'd keep studying with AI, and I'd help the older guys on the crew use it, because Mick still prints out his emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. I'd be worried for others more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Tony, who's been climbing for thirty years and can't stand screens. He knows more about these lines than any computer ever will, but if the company starts measuring everything by tablet, he'll look slow on paper. I'd want the union to make sure people like him aren't judged by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're upbeat here, but you also have thin savings. Does that worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, if I'm honest. If they cut the apprentice intake or slow the training, I can't afford even a few months without pay. But I've been broke before, with eight staff to pay, and I got through it, so the fear doesn't freeze me like it used to.

S1.say: This needs rules and unions at the table so the gains are shared, not just taken by shareholders. She would tell colleagues to learn the tools now.
S1.think: She thinks it could be good for her, because her brain is quicker than her hands and she is comfortable with technology. Drone and sensor work would suit her better than some older colleagues.
S1.do: Signs up for the drone pilot course in the first month and asks to join inspection trials. Joins or starts a union technology working group and helps older crewmates use AI.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, more worried for others than herself.
S1.quote: He knows more about these lines than any computer ever will, but if the company starts measuring everything by tablet, he'll look slow on paper.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima sees steady change as a chance to play to her strengths. She combines a pro-union view with real enthusiasm for the tools. When pressed on money she admits the fear, but her history of surviving a business failure keeps her steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when there are no rules, and governments let a few companies run ahead. I'd be calling for public control of it, honestly, and I'd say so at work. Online I'd be sharing everything about income support and how to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty, with a loan only just paid off, almost no pension and no savings. My drone course and my studying don't matter if the AI can fly the drone and the robot can frame the cross-arm. For the first time, I don't think being quick with technology saves me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for every short-term earning I could: storm overtime, weekend work. I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for a basic income or public ownership, because that's the only thing that would save people like me. I'd also ask the company about training to supervise the robots, even if it's just six months of work, because six months is six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. It's the speed. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being quick with technology doesn't save you. Is there anything that does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe people, more than skills. Joel's job at the school feels safer, kids still need a person there. And Amira, if she's in grid engineering, might be one of the people deciding how it all gets built. I hate the idea of leaning on my daughter, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two years of warning let you do, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, but I'd make sure the loan's done and I'd stop any spending that isn't food, rent or the car. I'd push my pension contributions up if I could, even a bit. Mostly it's time to make noise and join up with others.

S2.say: This is what happens when governments let a few companies run ahead with no rules. She would call for public control and share information on income support and organising.
S2.think: At sixty with almost no pension or savings, her skills with technology won't save her if AI can fly drones and robots can frame cross-arms. For the first time, being quick with tech doesn't feel like protection.
S2.do: Takes every bit of overtime and weekend work and joins campaigns for a basic income or public ownership. Asks the company about short-term work supervising robots, even for six months.
S2.feel: Frightened by the speed; two years feels like nothing.
S2.quote: For the first time, I don't think being quick with technology saves me.
S2.fieldNote: Fatima's optimism breaks in the fast scenario, because her edge with technology disappears if AI does everything. She turns to collective solutions and to her family, though she dislikes leaning on her daughter. Her practical streak still shows in grabbing any short-term work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so let's plan, and make the companies pay into it. At work I'd be pushing for a proper transition deal. Online I'd be more hopeful than in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, and I'd use that time to make myself one of the people who runs the new kit, not one replaced by it. It's not much time to build up savings, but it's enough to get a couple of qualifications. I'd also want to make sure I'm not the last one out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship and the drone licence in the first two years. I'd start a small side business doing drone surveys for farms out on the flats, weekends only, to build a cushion. I'd push the union for a fund that bridges older workers to their pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A drone survey business. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, maybe not. Farmers out past Saltmarsh already pay people to check crops and fences, and I've got eleven years of running a business, so I know how to price and invoice. The risk is the AI flies them itself by then, but I'd rather be in that market early than not at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Joel say about another business, after the last one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd groan and say not again, Fatima. Then he'd ask how much it costs, and when I said about two thousand for the drone and licence, he'd say fine, but we're not borrowing for it. That's fair; I'd save for it first.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to plan, and companies should pay into it. She would push for a proper transition deal and sound more hopeful than in the fast scenario.
S3.think: At sixty-three when it arrives, she wants to be one of the people who runs the new equipment. Five years is not much time to save, but enough for a couple of qualifications.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and drone licence within two years, then starts a weekend drone survey business for local farms, saving for the equipment first. Pushes the union for a pension bridge fund for older workers.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, and the busyness helps.
S3.quote: The risk is the AI flies them itself by then, but I'd rather be in that market early than not at all.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Fatima's entrepreneurial side comes back, drawing on her eleven years running a business. She is realistic that AI might take over drone work too, but would rather get in early. Her husband's caution keeps her from borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, if we use it. At work I'd say let's get training funded now, and get the pension rules sorted. Online I'd probably start a group for people retraining in their fifties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so I'd probably be retired before the worst of it, if the pension holds up. The bigger issue is building that pension in time, because I've got almost nothing in it. For me, the decade is mostly about money, not the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship, get qualified, and work as many years as I can on full lineworker pay to build the pension. I'd still do the drone course, and maybe the side business, to bring in extra. I'd tell Amira to look hard at which parts of engineering will still need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, about money more than anything. The work part I'm almost excited about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a group for people retraining in their fifties. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere people can admit they're scared and still learn something. I'd show them how I use the AI to study, because a lot of people my age think it's not for them. I'd call it something like Late Starters, because that's what we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to stay close to the decisions, not the drawings. If she's the one deciding where the lines go and who gets power, she matters even when the robots do the building. She'd probably tell me she already knew that, and she probably did.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, if we use it. She would push to fund training and fix pension rules, and might start an online group for people retraining in their fifties.
S4.think: At sixty-eight she would probably be retired before the worst, if her pension holds up. The real challenge is building that pension in time, since there is almost nothing in it.
S4.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and works as many years as possible on full lineworker pay to build her pension. Still takes the drone course and possibly the side business, and advises her daughter on her engineering career.
S4.feel: Uneasy about money, but almost excited about the work.
S4.quote: I'd call it something like Late Starters, because that's what we are.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Fatima's main concern is building a pension she barely has. She wants to help other older learners use AI, which fits her curious, generous nature. Her advice to her daughter shows she thinks about where human decisions still matter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I wouldn't have time to use the one advantage I have, which is that I'm not scared of new things. What would help is a basic income, or at least a bridge to pension for people my age, and free training that isn't just for young people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like to start a trade at fifty-five, and I'd say it's the best decision I've made in years. I just wish I'd made it at twenty-five. I spent eleven years cleaning other people's offices, and now I build the lines that light them.

headlineQuote: I spent eleven years cleaning other people's offices, and now I build the lines that light them.
portrait: Fatima Costa is a 58-year-old apprentice building new power lines out to solar farms, who came to the trade after her cleaning business failed in 2022. She is still paying off the business loan, has almost no pension, and lives with her husband Joel, a school caretaker; their daughter Amira studies electrical engineering. She uses AI every day to study and sees steady change as a chance to play to her strengths. The fast AGI picture shakes her badly, because her ease with technology no longer protects her. With more time she plans qualifications, a weekend drone survey business and, above all, building a pension.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because she wouldn't have time to use her one advantage, being unafraid of new things.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or a bridge to pension for people her age, and free training that isn't only for the young.
